claims.text: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can have a single-phase FCC structure.
Controlled thermomechanical processing produces the stated single-phase FCC initial state.
At least some ternary or quaternary subsets of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can remain single-phase FCC.
Changing the Mn and Fe ratios alters local lattice distortions.
Changing elemental ratios alters nanoscale chemical ordering or local chemical inhomogeneity.
Local chemical order changes the energy landscape and activation barriers experienced by moving dislocations.
Variations in local chemical order can change the operative deformation mechanisms and macroscopic strength, strain hardening, and ductility.
Concentration fluctuations can create variations in lattice friction that affect deformation behavior.
Enhanced local lattice distortion provides more effective dislocation-pinning sites and increases the critical resolved shear stress.
Greater local lattice distortion increases yield strength relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Greater local lattice distortion increases strain-hardening rates relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Reduced local lattice distortion lowers barriers to dislocation glide.
Reduced local lattice distortion produces lower strength but potentially greater ductility.

Mechanical properties need not improve simply with increasing constituent count, because an FCC ternary CrCoNi alloy can outperform the quinary alloy in cryogenic strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
Composition can be optimized by substituting expensive elements without sacrificing mechanical performance.
Specific compositional substitutions should improve the constituent-cost versus mechanical-performance trade-off.
The proposed interpretation is limited to processing and composition ranges that retain a stable single-phase FCC structure.
Secondary-phase formation can introduce additional mechanisms that invalidate the proposed single-phase interpretation.
The quantitative relationship among elemental variation, local distortion, and dislocation dynamics is not established.
